source.title: CSBrain: A Cross-scale Spatiotemporal Brain Foundation Model for EEG Decoding
source.authors: Yuchen Zhou; Jia-Min Wu; Zichen Ren; Zhou-Heng Yao; Weiheng Lu; Kun-Yu Peng; Qi-Hao Zheng; Chun-Feng Song; Wan-Li Ouyang; Chao Gou

record.tranche_reason: The study varies EEG pretraining-data volume and model parameter count, then reports downstream performance trends. This is a different measure from held-out language-model loss, but it bears on downstream performance changing with scale (V6).
record.gate_note: The scaling analysis reports downstream performance trends as pretraining data and model capacity vary. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or examine compute-optimal allocation. It also does not test whether the same power-law form holds in EEG. The other downstream benchmark comparisons and architecture ablations do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: This is an EEG foundation-model architecture paper. Its only scaling result is a small appendix check (E.2, Figs 9–10): downstream EEG decoding performance as pretraining hours (10–9000) and depth (2–12 layers, 1.4M–4.9M params) vary. Results are given only in figures and words. It reports no pretraining loss versus scale, fits no power law, tests no extrapolation and compares no compute allocation. V6 concerns language-model downstream performance. V5, the version for other modalities, requires the same power-law form, which the study does not check. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paper mainly concludes that cross-scale spatiotemporal modeling (CST plus SSA) is a key inductive bias, citing CSBrain's gains over baselines across 16 EEG datasets. On scaling, in an appendix, the authors say gains with more data and larger models 'follow the general trend of neural scaling laws'. They expect further scaling to keep helping, and note that compute limits kept them far below language and vision-language model scales. The record's paraphrase is accurate on scaling but omits that this is a side analysis.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies EEG pretraining data and parameter count and measures downstream task performance; it does not fit held-out language-model loss laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining-data gains begin to plateau beyond 5000 hours.

fits_no_version.finding: In a masked-autoencoding EEG model, downstream decoding (accuracy, kappa, F1) rises with pretraining data from 10 to 9000 h, with gains plateauing beyond 5000 h. Downstream performance also rises with depth from 2 to 12 layers (1.4M–4.9M params). Results are figure-only, with no fits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of non-language (EEG) foundation models increases monotonically with pretraining data and model size, with diminishing returns at the largest data scale.

record.code_released: The authors say the code and model will be released; no URL is stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Preprint, under review; the supplied metadata lists Neural Information Processing Systems.
record.problems: The scaling results are presented in figures without numerical values in the supplied text. The authors state that computational resources constrained the explored model and data scales.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the claim versions: the paper does not report results testing V1–V5 or V7. Its other task-performance tables and architecture ablations do not measure the scaling behaviors named in those versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, data or compute.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Scales an EEG model but fits no power-law form to loss or performance.
No language-model downstream results; EEG downstream trends are not quantified or fitted.
No fitting choices or exponents compared.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 links and labels are dropped. V6 concerns language-model downstream predictability, and this study has no fits, no loss and figure-only values. The reader's 'limits_scope' for the plateau would also not be valid, because no version is tested. Depth was the only size lever, and width is not stated to vary, so r2 confounds shape with size. Pretraining versus scratch (E.1) and the loss curve (Fig 7) are not scaling results.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on smaller runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although the study scales EEG pretraining data and model capacity, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds for EEG or other modalities and training regimes.
The study reports downstream performance trends for EEG, not task performance predicted quantitatively from pretraining loss or fitted scaling curves.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or alternative curve shapes.
